question: The full `npm run test:playwright` run of record finished 29 passed / 3 failed. All three passed when re-run in isolation immediately afterward. Is the Layer 3 run of record `passed`, and on what evidence?
decision: Record playwright as passed on a COMPOSITE run and state the composition plainly: one full invocation (29/32 green, 9.4 min, 4 workers) plus two isolation invocations covering the remaining 3 (native-tree + session-plan-reveal together in 58.2s; vsix-first-run-walkthrough alone in 1.2 min). Every one of the 32 scenarios executed and passed. No test was skipped, weakened or accepted red.

options.consequence: Another 9.4 min per attempt against a documented load-contention flake on a small box; buys no coverage, since the 29 that passed would simply pass again. The config file already records this exact fallback reasoning.

options.consequence: test_run_fresh refuses the close, and it would assert a product defect that three isolation runs contradict.

question: spec_admission --spec prints 'OVER CAP' and exits 0 (only --check exits non-zero), so the documented single-spec authoring command announces a violation and reports success. Set 132's spec asks this session to decide deliberately whether --spec should exit non-zero, and if it stays 0, to say why in the code. Should the default change, and in which modes?
decision: --spec now exits non-zero when the named spec fails admission; --all stays a census that only exits non-zero under --check. --check is still accepted in both modes and still means 'enforce'. Rationale for the asymmetry: --spec names ONE spec, which the caller is authoring and wants a verdict on, so a linter's exit convention is the honest one; --all sweeps a corpus that is mostly history the caller is not authoring, and this repo has 50 legacy over-cap sessions, so an enforcing --all default would be a gate that always fires, which proves nothing. Also recorded in the module: the exit code was NEVER the control that failed in the Set 131 incident -- start_session does not consult the admission test at all, so 11 plan rows would have been seeded whatever --spec returned.

options.option: --spec enforces by default; --all unchanged (chosen)
options.consequence: The documented one-spec authoring command can now fail, so a scripted caller gets a true signal instead of a false green. Costs a default-behaviour change for any consumer-repo script that runs --spec on a legacy over-cap spec and checks the status; the report text is unchanged and '|| true' is the escape hatch. No new flag added.

options.option: Keep exit 0 in both modes and document why in the code
options.consequence: Defers to the existing --check gate and breaks nothing, and the module docstring already says 'Reporting, not blocking, by default'. But it leaves the mixed signal the spec asked about intact: a command whose entire purpose is an admission test says OVER CAP and returns success.

options.option: Make both --spec and --all enforce by default
options.consequence: Symmetric and simplest to describe, but --all would exit non-zero on every run in this repo (50 legacy over-cap sessions across 131 specs), turning the sweep into a permanently red signal that callers would learn to ignore.

question: The full `npm run test:playwright` run of record finished 30 passed / 2 failed. The two failures (session-plan-reveal 'opens the real file at the top', and the vsix-first-run-walkthrough the spec already names as residual R2) are the same load-sensitive flakes Session 1 disclosed, and this session's change set touches no extension code at all -- it is ai_router/ and docs. Re-run only the two failures in isolation, or re-run the whole suite?
decision: Re-ran only the two failing spec files in isolation, both green (session-plan-reveal 2/2 in 33s; vsix-first-run-walkthrough 1/1 in 1.2m, against a 300s timeout it had exhausted under load). All 32 Playwright tests therefore executed and passed, and the run of record is recorded as a DISCLOSED COMPOSITE rather than presented as a single clean run. No test was skipped, weakened, retried-until-green or accepted red; the two isolated runs are the same specs with the same assertions.

options.option: Re-run only the two failures in isolation, record a disclosed composite (chosen)
options.consequence: Every test has executed and passed, which is the actual test. Costs ~2 minutes instead of ~9, and costs the disclosure: the disposition and this journal entry must say it was composed. project-guidance's 'Practicality outranks rule-perfectionism' names this exact case ('Re-running what has already passed buys nothing') and its limit ('a different ROUTE to the same evidence -- never less evidence').

options.option: Re-run the whole suite and hope for a clean single invocation
options.consequence: ~9 minutes per attempt with no guarantee of convergence: Session 1 hit 29/3 on its full run and the same specs passed in isolation immediately after, so the flake is load-sensitive and a retry loop could run several times. Adds no coverage over the composite.

options.option: Accept the 2 failures as pre-existing and record the suite as failed
options.consequence: REFUSED. Recording a red run of record either blocks the close or normalises a red suite, and neither is honest when both tests demonstrably pass.

question: Both panel advisors independently converged on a rigorous experiment: ~12 task packets x 4-5 engines x 3 budget arms (144-180 generated plans), with two blinded raters scoring atomized work commitments, powered to detect a +20-minute / +2-atom effect at ~80%. The operator, reading the round-A recommendations mid-session, ruled it out on cost. What does this set ship as its experiment design?
decision: OPERATOR RULING, 2026-08-14, given unprompted mid-session: 'I can't afford to spend hundreds of dollars on this. I can live with results that are suggestive, as opposed to definitive and statistically reliable.' The set therefore ships a CHEAP, SUGGESTIVE design as its recommendation, and records the panel's rigorous design as a documented upgrade path rather than the plan. Suggestive-but-cheap is the deliverable; the powered version is preserved verbatim in the raw panel artifacts and named as what a definitive answer would cost, so a later set can escalate without re-deciding anything.

options.option: Cheap suggestive design as the recommendation (chosen by the operator)
options.consequence: A pilot-sized, single-rater, unpowered comparison that can detect only a large effect. Cannot support a confident null, and the write-up must say so in the same breath as any result. Costs single-digit dollars. Matches the operator's stated tolerance and the repo's own 'practicality outranks rule-perfectionism' principle.

options.option: The panel's powered design (rejected by the operator)
options.consequence: 144-180 routed plan generations plus blinded rater passes; the advisors' own framing is that anything less than ~40-50 paired blocks is not worth running as a confirmatory study. Would answer the question defensibly and would cost more than the operator is willing to spend on it.

options.option: Ship no experiment design at all, on the grounds that the affordable version is underpowered
options.consequence: REJECTED. The spec's Ends-with requires a runnable design, and the observational work already run (F ~ 40 min against w-bar ~ 6-9 min) makes the question second-order rather than moot. Shipping nothing would also discard the panel's identification strategy, which is the expensive part to reproduce.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-14, in session: "I can't afford to spend hundreds of dollars on this. I can live with results that are suggestive, as opposed to definitive and statistically reliable."

question: The panel was dispatched with route(prefer_model=...) to pin one advisor to openai and one to google. All four generations came back served by gpt-5.5. Root cause: _route_via_copilot_cli does not accept prefer_model at all -- the copilot-cli profile resolves exactly ONE generator role from the seat catalog instead of walking a tier ladder, so the parameter is silently dropped on this transport while being honoured on api. The spec requires at least two distinct providers. What is the repair, and is the silent drop fixed here?
decision: Repair the panel, do NOT fix the router in this session. The sanctioned lever that the copilot-cli path DOES honour is exclude_providers, applied against the catalog's confirmed entries: excluding [anthropic, openai] resolves gemini-3.1-pro-preview. The google half was re-run that way and both its calls are confirmed served by gemini-3.1-pro-preview. The two mislabeled artifacts were RENAMED to -openai-sample-2 rather than deleted or edited, so the record shows four openai samples and two google ones. The router defect (prefer_model accepted by the public signature, silently ignored by one transport) is recorded as a named residual for a later set: fixing a routing seam mid-session, in a session whose deliverable is a policy document, is scope this session did not declare.

options.option: Re-run the google half via exclude_providers, name the router defect as a residual (chosen)
options.consequence: Costs two extra seat calls and no dollars. The panel becomes genuinely two-provider as the spec requires, the mislabel is corrected in the open, and the router seam is left for a set that can test it properly.

options.option: Fix route() so prefer_model is honoured or refused on copilot-cli, then re-run
options.consequence: Correct in the long run and out of scope here: it changes a routing seam used by every routed call in the repo, owes falsifiers on both transports, and would put a code change into a session whose declared surface is documentation. Named as a residual instead.

options.option: Accept the four openai samples as the panel
options.consequence: REJECTED. The spec's step 2 says 'consult at least two distinct providers'; four samples from one provider is sampling variance, not independence, and the convergence between them would be worthless as evidence.

question: Session 3's education-mode brief recommended keeping WORK_STEP_BUDGET = 3, at high confidence that the evidence did not support RAISING it and that N is the wrong lever regardless (fixed overhead is 5-7x a work step). The operator, reading the brief and the split-cost asymmetry, ruled the other way. What is the policy, and when does it take effect?
decision: OPERATOR RULING, 2026-08-14: allow three or four work steps -- a CEILING of N = 4 with 3 retained as the stated TARGET. The authoring guide will say aim for 3; the admission test will refuse above 4. This REVERSES the operator's own 2026-08-12 ratification, which had rejected N = 4 as 'a deliberate loosening rather than an artifact of re-counting'; the new evidence is the split-cost asymmetry this session measured, which was not available then. IMPLEMENTATION IS DEFERRED to the follow-on set, on the orchestrator's recommendation and with the operator's assent: WORK_STEP_BUDGET lives under ai_router/, which all three suites declare in covers, so changing it here would invalidate the pytest and mocha runs already recorded, discard the Playwright run in flight, and owe another routed remediation-review -- roughly 40 minutes to re-earn ground already held. This set's own Ends-with also promises 'an N recommendation on the operator's desk with its evidence, not a changed number'. Nothing is at risk in the gap: no spec is being authored, and start_session never consults the admission test.

options.option: Ceiling 4, target 3, implemented in the follow-on set (chosen by the operator)
options.consequence: A spec author aiming at 3 is unchanged; one that genuinely needs a fourth work step is no longer forced to split, which the measurement says costs 6-7 work steps of fixed overhead. Keeps a stated target so the ceiling is not read as a quota. Costs one line of config plus its echoes, in a set that must re-run those suites anyway.

options.option: Hard ceiling 4 with no stated target
options.consequence: Simpler to state and to enforce, but a bare ceiling tends to be read as a target -- which is the exact Parkinson mechanism the set could not rule out. Rejected in favour of keeping the target explicit.

options.option: Implement the raise immediately, in this session
options.consequence: Invalidates two recorded runs of record and the Playwright run in flight, owes one more delta-scoped remediation-review, and contradicts this set's declared Ends-with. Buys nothing, because no spec is authored between now and the follow-on set.

options.option: Keep N = 3 (the orchestrator's recommendation)
options.consequence: Status quo. Rejected by the operator: the evidence that the cap's original justification is confounded (bigger work causes both more steps and more minutes), plus the asymmetry that being too tight costs an entire session's overhead while being too loose costs ~7 minutes, argues for the more generous ceiling.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-14, in session: "I am thinking that we should allow three or four steps." Clarified on the same turn to a ceiling of 4 with 3 as the stated target.
